question: How does contemplation of the great lake of supreme consciousness lead to the experience of mantra-power and conclude the first unfolding?
premises: Supreme consciousness is likened to a great lake because it emits the universe while remaining clear, uncovered, and deep.
Inward, uninterrupted contemplation of identity with that consciousness yields the manifestation of full I-consciousness as the power of all mantras.
The same supreme power appears as mātṛkā and mālinī, and its recognition removes bondage and grants attainments in the śāmbhava unfolding.
inference: Therefore, by contemplative absorption in the supreme power as the great lake, one directly experiences mantra-power as one's own full I-consciousness, which pacifies bondage and completes the first śāmbhava unfolding.

The fragment 'mātṛkā##tadākramya' at token 94 appears as a fused citation form; its precise syntactic role depends on the omitted surrounding quotation.
plain_english: Kṣemarāja explains that supreme consciousness is like a vast lake: it gives rise to the whole universe, from will down to the grossest objects, yet remains clear, uncovered, and unfathomably deep. By turning inward and steadily contemplating one's identity with that consciousness, one comes to experience the power of mantra as the living presence of full I-consciousness, the great mantra behind all mantras. He supports this with the Mālinīvijaya, showing that the same supreme power appears as mātṛkā and mālinī, the source of all mantras and knowledge. Recognizing this power dissolves bondage rooted in non-recognition of consciousness, transforms the world into the nectar of one's own bliss, and grants all attainments. The passage closes by identifying this as the first unfolding, the śāmbhava means, grounded in Śiva's freedom and power.
